The most important map of the 21st century isn't about war, oil or borders.

It's about babies.

Niger: ~6 births per woman. South Korea: ~0.7. Everything about the year 2100 is hiding in this gap.

One data map, explained — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ The magic number is 2.1 — the fertility rate that keeps a population stable.

On the map, almost everything outside Africa is now below it: the Americas, all of Europe, East Asia, most of the Middle East and India.

That would have been unthinkable in 1950.

2/ In 1950, the global average was about 5 children per woman. Today it's roughly 2.2 and falling.

In historical terms this is an eyeblink — the fastest voluntary change in human reproduction ever recorded.

3/ Why does it fall? The pattern repeats everywhere: children stop dying, girls go to school, families move to cities — and births drop.

Iran went from ~6.5 to ~1.7 in a single generation. No coercion required; it happens on every continent, in every religion.

4/ The extreme case: South Korea, ~0.7.

At that rate each generation is about a third the size of the one before. 100 Koreans have ~33 children and ~11 grandchildren.

China, Japan, Italy and Spain are all on the same slope — China's population is already shrinking.

5/ The other pole: the Sahel and Central Africa — Niger, Chad, DR Congo, Somalia — still at 5-6+.

UN projections put ~1 in 3 humans in Africa by 2100. The century's migrations, markets and militaries are all written in this map.

6/ Empires used to compete for territory. The 21st century's quiet contest is demographic — and the map above is its scoreboard.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
